guglielmo_and_malle_2019_actual_findings.summary: Guglielmo & Malle (2019) tested two distinct hypotheses across four studies (Studies 1-4): (1) the 'amplified blame hypothesis', that people assign more intense blame to an actor performing (or mentally committing to) a negative behavior than praise to an actor performing (or committing to) a positive behavior WHEN the negative and positive behaviors are pretested and matched on basic extremity (degree of negativity vs. positivity); and (2) the 'differentiated blame hypothesis', that people distinguish more finely among pre-action mental commitment stages (thinking about vs. wanting vs. planning/intending to act) for blame than for praise. Across Studies 1-4, participants rated single agents on intensity/amount of blame or praise (e.g., -5 to +5 commensurable scale in Study 1; 0-7 unipolar scales in Study 2; 0-100 slider scales in Study 3 and Study 4) across extremity-matched behavior sets and manipulated mental-state commitment levels. They found narrow/partial support for amplified blame (random-effects meta-analysis across seven subsamples in Studies 1-4: d = 0.34, 95% CI [0.038, 0.641], z = 2.21, p = .027, supported in Studies 1, 3, and 4B while null in Studies 2 and 4A) and consistent, robust support for differentiated blame across mental states (average d = 0.67).

proofs.literal_contiguous_quote:
Citation: Guglielmo S, Malle BF (2019) Asymmetric
morality: Blame is more differentiated and more
extreme than praise. PLoS ONE 14(3): e0213544.
https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0213544

Despite extensive recent investigations of moral judgments, little is known about how negative judgments like blame might differ from positive judgments like praise. Drawing on theory
from both social and moral cognition, the present studies identify and test potential asymmetries in the extremity and differentiatedness of blame as compared to praise. The amplified
blame hypothesis predicts that people will assign greater blame for negative behaviors than
praise for positive behaviors. The differentiated blame hypothesis predicts that, as compared to praise judgments, blame judgments will more finely differentiate among distinct
mental states that precede action, such as thoughts, desires, and intentions. A series of
studies—using varied stimulus sets and samples—together provide robust support for the
differentiated blame hypothesis and somewhat weaker support for the amplified blame
hypotheses. These results illustrate systematic asymmetries between blame and praise,
generally revealing that blame is more extreme and differentiated than praise. Together, the
findings reflect the social costs and social regulatory function of moral judgments, suggesting that blame and praise are not mirror images and that blame might be more complex.

We present a series of studies designed to test two potential asymmetries between moral judgments of blame versus praise. The amplified blame hypothesis predicts that, even when
matched on their overall basic extremity, negative behaviors will elicit more blame than positive behaviors will elicit praise. We test this hypothesis in Studies 1, 2, 3, and 4. The differentiated blame hypothesis predicts that people’s blame judgments, compared with praise

PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0213544 March 12, 2019

3 / 20

 Blame differs from praise

judgments, will more finely differentiate among distinct levels of commitment to bringing
about an action or outcome. We test this hypothesis in three studies, first with a smaller set of
such levels (thinking and intending: Study 1) and then an expanded set (thinking, wanting,
and planning: Studies 2 and 3).

Participants answered three questions, in a fixed order, about each item: blame/praise
(“How much blame or praise would someone deserve if the person thought about [behavior
statement] / intended to [behavior statement] / [behavior statement]”), likelihood of performing
(asked only in the thinking and intending conditions: “How likely is it that the person would
actually [behavior statement]”), and basic extremity (“Overall, how socially negative or positive
is it for a person to [behavior statement]”). The blame/praise and basic extremity questions
were answered on a -5 (a lot of blame/very negative) to +5 (a lot of praise/very positive) scale,
and the likelihood question on a 0 (very unlikely) to 6 (very likely) scale. We then reversed the
sign of blame ratings and extremity ratings for all negative items so that blame and praise ratings, as well as extremity ratings, were on a commensurable scale across valence.

We then assessed our primary hypotheses. Since our items were now appropriately equated
on basic extremity across valence (e.g., the most extreme negative and positive items were designated as item 1), we now included random intercepts for items as well. Thus, we tested the
amplified blame hypothesis with a mixed-effects model predicting item-level moral judgment
ratings by valence, including random intercepts for subjects and for items. R syntax: lmer
(rating~valence+(1|subj)+(1|item)). Surprisingly, blame ratings were no higher (M = 4.21,
SD = 2.32) than praise ratings (M = 3.99, SD = 2.32), t = .20, p = .85, ds = .34 (between-subjects
comparison in the single valence conditions) and -.06 (within-subjects comparison in the dual
valence condition), counter to the blame amplification prediction.

This article reported a series of studies designed to test potential asymmetries between moral
judgments of blame and praise. The results revealed systematic ways in which these judgments
differ. Blame tended to be more extreme than praise, even when behaviors were matched on
degree of basic extremity. Blame was more differentiated: people made more fine-grained distinctions among particular mental states (i.e., thinking vs. wanting vs. intending) when assigning blame than when assigning praise. Together, these findings reflect the social costs and
social regulatory function of moral judgments, suggesting that blame and praise are not mirror
images and that blame might be more complex.

w34fb_report_actual_usage_and_hypothesis.summary: In w34fb.report.txt, Tsang & Feldman explicitly designate Gray et al. (2011) Experiments Four and Five as their sole replication target (p. 2, p. 5, p. 8, Tables 1-3, Table 13) and frame Hypotheses 8-13 as extensions of Gray et al.'s (2011) second effect (that body focus increases perceived moral patiency and decreases perceived moral agency). In the Introduction subsection 'Comparison of Moral Praiseworthiness and Blameworthiness' (p. 13), the authors cite Anderson et al.'s (2020) review and Guglielmo & Malle (2019) as background premises, reinterpreting Guglielmo & Malle's term 'differentiated' (which in Guglielmo & Malle meant distinguishing among thinking/wanting/planning mental states) as 'a higher degree of certainty in the differentiation', and explicitly deduce a new prediction about target-selection certainty: 'Taking the above, we deduced that people are more certain in the attribution of moral blameworthiness than moral praiseworthiness. In other words, we reckon that it is easier for people to identify which person is morally blameworthy than which person is praiseworthy.' Empirically, in Experiment 5 (pp. 21-23, 32-38), participants view two targets—Jeffrey (Mind Target) and Michael (Body Target)—who BOTH perform the exact same negative behavior ('They both walk out of a restaurant without paying, if one of them deserved more blame, who would it be?') and BOTH perform the exact same positive behavior ('They both helped a child get out of danger, if one of them deserved more praise, who would it be?'). There is no extremity matching between walking out of a restaurant without paying and helping a child out of danger, no manipulation of pre-action mental commitment stages, and no measure of the amount/severity of blame or praise deserved for the act. Instead, participants answer on Gray et al.'s (2011) 6-point forced-choice relative target-selection scale (-2.5 = Definitely Michael, -1.5 = Probably Michael, -0.5 = Possibly Michael, +0.5 = Possibly Jeffrey, +1.5 = Probably Jeffrey, +2.5 = Definitely Jeffrey), where magnitude |X| in {0.5, 1.5, 2.5} indexes decision certainty ('Possibly' vs. 'Probably' vs. 'Definitely') in choosing between the Mind-focused and Body-focused target (Figure 5 Note, p. 36). Hypothesis 10 takes the absolute value |X| of those forced-choice target-preference ratings (M = 0.77, SD = 0.53 for blame vs. M = 0.73, SD = 0.49 for praise; paired t(1008) = 2.60, p = .005, d = 0.08). Finally, in the Discussion of Hypothesis 10 (pp. 48-49), Guglielmo & Malle (2019) is not cited or mentioned at all; the result is discussed exclusively via Anderson et al. (2020) and primary papers cited therein (Gneezy & Epley, 2014; Klein & Epley, 2014; Klein & O'Brien, 2016; Monroe et al., 2018; Siegel et al., 2017; Barasch et al., 2016; Berman et al., 2015) as showing the difficulty of praise vs. blame attribution.

proofs.literal_contiguous_quote:
Revisiting the link between Mind Perception and Objectification:
               Replication and Extension of Gray et al (2011)

Citation of the target research article:

        Gray, K., Knobe, J., Sheskin, M., Bloom, P., & Barrett, L. F. (2011). More than a body:
        Mind perception and the nature of objectification. Journal of Personality and Social
        Psychology, 101(6), 1207–1220. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0025883

Extending the replication, we failed to find support for a lower

perceived moral praiseworthiness or a higher perceived capacity to feel pleasure with increased

body focus. However, we found support for a higher attribution of moral blameworthiness than

moral praiseworthiness, a positive association between perceived moral blameworthiness and

perceived free will, and increased perceived agency and experience with mind focus.

The study described in the current paper is a very close replication of Gray et al.’s (2011)

study and had two clear goals. The first goal is to conduct independent close replications of the two

effects. The second goal is to extend the second effect to provide more clarity and reveal its

potential complexity.

Comparison of Moral Praiseworthiness and Blameworthiness


       A recent review by Anderson et al. (2020) suggested that, as compared to positive outcomes,

observers tend to evaluate negative outcomes of a moral act more strongly, despite the equal

magnitude of the outcome impacts. In other words, “moral wrongs are seen as more objectively

wrong than moral goods are seen as objectively right” (p. 6). Moreover, Guglielmo and Malle

(2019) illustrated that blame is consistently more extreme and differentiated than praise. In other

words, as compared to praise, people seem to blame more severely with a higher degree of certainty

in the differentiation. Taking the above, we deduced that people are more certain in the attribution

of moral blameworthiness than moral praiseworthiness. In other words, we reckon that it is easier

for people to identify which person is morally blameworthy than which person is praiseworthy.

People judge negative moral acts more strongly than positive moral
Extension on 5       10        acts. Specifically, attribution of moral blameworthiness is greater than
                               attribution of moral praiseworthiness.

DV1: Moral agency - Moral blameworthiness
Specific DV item: “They both walk out of a restaurant without paying, if one of them deserved more
blame, who would it be?”

DV2: Moral patiency – Capacity to be harmed
Specific DV item: “They both were attacked by a mugger, if one of them suffered more harm at the hands
of the mugger, who would it be?”

(Extension) DV3: Moral agency - Moral praiseworthiness
Specific DV item: “They both helped a child get out of danger, if one of them deserved more praise, who
would it be?”

All the DVs 1 to 6 above are on a six-point scale (-2.5 = Definitely Michael, -1.5 = Probably Michael, -
0.5 = Possibly Michael, +0.5 = Possibly Jeffrey, +1.5 = Probably Jeffrey, +2.5 = Definitely Jeffrey; with a
hypothetical midpoint of equality/indifference at zero). Such forced-choice scale without the choice of
equality/indifference was the same scale used in previous related research and correlated well with other
measures (Gray et al., 2011; Gray & Wegner, 2009).

Note. All the scale was from –2.5 = Definitely Michael to +2.5 = Definitely Jeffrey with a hypothetical
midpoint of zero/equality/indifference. Positive values indicate that Mind Target (Jeffrey) was perceived to
have more of the characteristic than was Body Target (Michael); negative values indicate that Body Target
was perceived to have more of the characteristic than was Mind Target. Higher magnitude indicates higher
certainty in the attribution of the characteristic.

We conducted one-sample t-tests (Student’s t, two-tailed). We failed to find support for

Hypothesis 8 that people tended to consider Mind Target to be more morally praiseworthy (M =

0.03, SD = 0.88; t(1008) = 0.95, p = .341; Cohen’s d = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.03, 0.09]).

We conducted a paired samples t-test (Student’s t, two-tailed) and found support for

Hypothesis 10 that moral blameworthiness (in absolute value; M = 0.77, SD = 0.53) is larger than

moral praiseworthiness (in absolute value; M = 0.73, SD = 0.49; t(1008) = 2.60, p = .005; Cohen’s d

= 0.08, 95% CI [0.02, 0.14]).

 Moral praiseworthiness        0.73 0.49    2.60     1008       .005      0.05       d = 0.08 [0.02, 0.14]
  - 10 (Extension)

We found support for Hypothesis 10 that there is stronger attribution of moral

blameworthiness than moral praiseworthiness. This result is in line with Anderson et al. ’s (2020)

review that the attribution of moral agent’s praise and blame are not symmetrical (Gneezy & Epley,

2014; Klein & Epley, 2014; Klein & O’Brien, 2016; Monroe et al., 2018; Siegel et al., 2017); that

is, not with the same magnitude of different directions. People seem to have different sensitivities to

the extent of the moral outcome. Specifically, when they are to give blame or praise, they seem to

be more sensitive to the degree of harm caused than to the benefits of positive behavior - also

signifies the ‘negative bias’ (Anderson et al., 2020; Goodwin & Darley, 2012; Klein & O’Brien,

2016; Rozin & Royzman, 2001). Moreover, Anderson et al. indicated that people based more on the

outcome when attributing blame. And when it comes to praise, they base more on the target’s

underlying motivation and attitude (Barasch et al., 2016; Berman et al., 2015; Berman & Small,

2018; Carlson & Zaki, 2018). For example, when people make moral praise judgments, they tend to

question: “Are they good persons?” instead of “Is this a good action?”; people tend to think:

“Although it is a good deed, they are not praiseworthy if they are driven by self-interest, I am not

sure if this good act is out of genuinely prosocial or altruistic motive.”. On the other hand, moral

blame judgments are more outcome-oriented and direct: ‘Wrong is wrong, even though they did not

intend to.’ (Anderson et al., 2020). As such, this highlighted the difficulty in making praise

attribution as compared to blame attribution.

adjudication.rationale: Under Codebook Step 2, a cited study is a replication target only if THIS paper re-tests its reported empirical finding with its own data ('A study cited for background, motivation or context is NOT a target'; 'A listed reference is a target only when THIS paper itself re-tests its finding. A work cited as background, as commentary, or as an earlier replication attempt that this paper does not itself re-test is NOT a target, even when its title names the same effect, gene or phenomenon... The evidence_quote for a target must show the paper stating that it re-tests that work'). Joint reading of w34fb.report.txt and Guglielmo & Malle (2019) establishes that Guglielmo & Malle (2019) is cited solely as background motivation (alongside the review article Anderson et al., 2020) to deduce a novel extension hypothesis inside Gray et al.'s (2011) Experiment Five Mind-vs.-Body target comparison paradigm, rather than being empirically re-tested: (1) Explicit deductive shift in the Introduction: After summarizing Anderson et al. (2020) and Guglielmo & Malle (2019) ('blame is consistently more extreme and differentiated than praise'), Tsang & Feldman gloss 'differentiated' as 'a higher degree of certainty in the differentiation' and write: 'Taking the above, we deduced that people are more certain in the attribution of moral blameworthiness than moral praiseworthiness. In other words, we reckon that it is easier for people to identify which person is morally blameworthy than which person is praiseworthy.' (2) Fundamental construct and operational mismatch with Guglielmo & Malle (2019): Guglielmo & Malle tested whether blame intensity exceeds praise intensity across negative and positive behaviors pretested and matched on basic extremity (amplified blame) and whether blame differentiates more finely across pre-action mental commitment stages (thinking about vs. wanting vs. planning/intending; differentiated blame). Tsang & Feldman's Experiment 5 does not match the extremity of its two vignettes (walking out of a restaurant without paying vs. helping a child out of danger), does not manipulate mental commitment stages, and does not measure the amount of blame or praise assigned to an act. Instead, both targets (Jeffrey and Michael) commit the same act, and participants rate 'who deserved more blame/praise' on Gray et al.'s 6-point forced-choice scale (-2.5 Definitely Michael to +2.5 Definitely Jeffrey). Taking the absolute value |X| in {0.5, 1.5, 2.5} measures decision certainty (Possibly = 0.5, Probably = 1.5, Definitely = 2.5) in discriminating between a Mind-focused and a Body-focused target, which is an extension of Gray et al.'s (2011) mind-perception paradigm, not a conceptual replication of Guglielmo & Malle (2019). (3) Total absence from Discussion and replication benchmarks: Guglielmo & Malle (2019) is mentioned once in the Introduction (p. 13) and listed in the References (p. 64). It is never mentioned in Methods, Results, Table 13 (which summarizes replication outcomes exclusively for Gray et al.'s Hypotheses 1-7), or Discussion (pp. 48-49, which discusses Hypothesis 10 exclusively in relation to Anderson et al.'s 2020 review and other papers cited via Anderson et al., without mentioning Guglielmo & Malle 2019).

strongest_alternative.case_for_alternative: The strongest case for coding Guglielmo & Malle (2019) as a second target (and therefore 'genuinely_missing', since no row in flora_b48a7d6.csv or handoff files pairs W34FB/8HDU3 with 10.1371/journal.pone.0213544) rests on three points: (a) Codebook Step 2 & Step 3 state that 'Judge the RELATIONSHIP, not the wording — a paper that tests whether a specific published result holds in a new sample is a replication whether or not it uses the word "replication"' and 'a conceptual replication re-tests the original's claim by design'; (b) while the Introduction prose on p. 13 shifts to target-identification certainty, the formal wording of Hypothesis 10 in Table 3 (p. 16), the Abstract (p. 4), the Results heading (p. 37), and the Discussion (p. 48) is stated broadly as 'People judge negative moral acts more strongly than positive moral acts. Specifically, attribution of moral blameworthiness is greater than attribution of moral praiseworthiness'; and (c) in the two-citation background paragraph on p. 13, Anderson et al. (2020) is a review paper (ruled out as a target by Codebook Step 2), leaving Guglielmo & Malle (2019) as the only cited primary empirical study supporting the blame-more-extreme-than-praise proposition. If Guglielmo & Malle (2019) were treated as a conceptual-replication target for Hypothesis 10, its conditional replication outcome in w34fb.report.txt would be 'successful' because the authors explicitly report statistical support for Hypothesis 10 (M = 0.77 vs. M = 0.73, t(1008) = 2.60, p = .005, d = 0.08).
strongest_alternative.why_alternative_is_rejected: The alternative is rejected because broad summary phrasing in Table 3 ('judge negative moral acts more strongly than positive moral acts') cannot override how the authors explicitly derived and operationalized the test. First, on p. 13 the authors explicitly mark their step from Guglielmo & Malle's finding to Hypothesis 10 as a deductive inference to a different construct ('Taking the above, we deduced that people are more certain in the attribution of moral blameworthiness than moral praiseworthiness. In other words, we reckon that it is easier for people to identify which person is morally blameworthy than which person is praiseworthy'). Second, the empirical test (|X| in {0.5, 1.5, 2.5} on a forced-choice comparison between two targets who both committed the same unmatched act) cannot test Guglielmo & Malle's amplified blame hypothesis (which requires extremity-matched positive and negative acts and a measure of blame/praise severity) or differentiated blame hypothesis (which requires manipulating mental commitment stages). Third, the authors themselves do not treat Hypothesis 10 as a re-test of Guglielmo & Malle (2019), omitting Guglielmo & Malle (2019) entirely from the Results and Discussion. Under Codebook Step 2 ('A study cited for background, motivation or context is NOT a target' and 'Do NOT include a study because it is topically similar, prominent, frequently cited, or the only option offered'), Guglielmo & Malle (2019) is a non-target background citation, parallel to Genschow & Vehlow (2021) for Hypothesis 11.

codebook_proofs.literal_contiguous_quote:
What counts as a target:
- The paper must re-test that study's reported finding: collecting new data to check
  whether it holds, or re-analysing that study's own data. Judge the RELATIONSHIP,
  not the wording — a paper that tests whether a specific published result holds in a
  new sample is a replication whether or not it uses the word "replication". A study
  cited for background, motivation or context is NOT a target.
- Do NOT include a study because it is topically similar, prominent, frequently
  cited, or the only option offered.
- A listed reference is a target only when THIS paper itself re-tests its finding. A
  work cited as background, as commentary, or as an earlier replication attempt that
  this paper does not itself re-test is NOT a target, even when its title names the
  same effect, gene or phenomenon. An earlier replication attempt CAN be the target —
  when this paper re-tests IT. What decides is what this paper does with the work, not
  what kind of work the citation is. The evidence_quote for a target must show the
  paper stating that it re-tests that work.

- Replication chains: when the finding has already been re-tested by others, the
  target is the study closest to this paper in the chain — the one it actually
  re-tests — not the chain's original source.

Before naming any entry, rule out: another work by the same authors; a registered-report protocol or preregistration versus the paper reporting the original finding; the paper that supplied the materials, task or measure versus the finding re-tested; a meta-analysis or review versus the primary study; a meeting abstract or working paper versus the published article.

A changed method, measure, paradigm, population or setting does not by itself mean the paper
has not compared: a conceptual replication re-tests the original's claim by design, and rule 2
applies to it unchanged.
